本当.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 本 ('root, origin, true') and 当 ('hit the mark, right, proper'). Historical dictionaries record 本当 in the sense of 'truth' in a 1770 work and 'a genuine or proper state' in a 1785 work; the shorter colloquial form ほんと arose by vowel shortening from ほんとう.

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 本当

の.etymology: Native Japanese genitive and noun-linking particle already attested in the Kojiki (712). Over time it also developed a nominalizing function turning clauses into noun-like statements; in modern spoken Japanese, explanatory の before です or だ frequently contracts to ん.

history.meaning: links a modifying noun to a following noun

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — の

自分.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 自 ('oneself') and 分 ('portion, lot, status'). Historical dictionaries document self-referring uses in a diary entry dated 1425 as well as uses pointing to the person concerned; its reference shifts naturally with speaker and context.

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 自分

だ.etymology: Plain copula formed by phonological contraction of である to であ and then だ during the Muromachi period, especially in eastern Japanese speech (with cited examples from 1473 onward).

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — だ

いる.etymology: Spelled ゐる (wiru) prior to modern kana reform. Originally meaning 'to sit down' or 'stay still in one spot' in contrast with standing, it broadened into the standard verb of animate existence ('be present, stay') and progressive aspect.

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 居る

なる.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *naru*, attested in eighth-century texts for coming into being, bearing fruit, and changing into another state. Its modern everyday sense 'become' continues that core change-of-state meaning.

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 成る

から.etymology: Case and conjunctive particle with older spatial and temporal uses marking a starting point or route ('from'). Its causal clause use ('because, since') developed in Early Modern Japanese, with dictionary citations from around 1710.

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — から

ほしい.etymology: Descends from Old Japanese adjective *fosi* (classical ほし), attested in the Kojiki and Man'yōshū in the sense of 'desirable, wanted'. Modern ほしい (欲しい) generalized the attributive *-ki > -i* ending, and the auxiliary request pattern 〜てほしい is attested by 1686.

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 欲しい

です.etymology: Polite copula documented from the Muromachi period onward that spread across general polite speech in the late Edo and Meiji periods. Reference dictionaries list several proposed contractions—including で候 (de sōrō), でおはす, でございます, and であります—without consensus on a single source.

history.meaning: stylized copular ending in dramatic and social registers

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — です

に.etymology: Core Japanese case particle attested throughout eighth-century Man'yōshū poetry, marking points in time, static locations of existence, destinations, and indirect recipients.

history.meaning: marks location, time, goal, and recipient

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — に

また.etymology: Native adverb attested in the Nihon Shoki (720) meaning 'again, once more', later extending to 'also' and 'on another occasion'—the sense underlying everyday farewells like またね ('see you again') and また明日 ('see you tomorrow').

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 又

ね.etymology: Sentence-final conversational particle documented from late Edo speech (with dictionary citations from 1788), used to invite agreement, confirm shared information, or soften a statement.

sources.title: Shogakukan: Digital Daijisen / Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — ね

パン.etymology: Borrowed in the sixteenth century from Portuguese pão ('bread'), introduced by Portuguese traders and missionaries in Nagasaki and remaining one of Japanese's oldest everyday European loanwords.

コーヒー.etymology: Borrowed in the late Edo period from Dutch koffie ('coffee') through the Dutch trading post at Dejima in Nagasaki; scholars also coined the phonetic kanji spelling 珈琲.

ガラス.etymology: Borrowed in the Edo period from Dutch glas ('glass'), referring to sheet and window glass as a material (whereas the later English borrowing グラス denotes a drinking glass).

コップ.etymology: Borrowed from Dutch kop (or Portuguese copo) during the early modern trade era to name a tumbler or drinking cup without a handle.

スーツケース.etymology: Borrowed from English suitcase ('flat-sided Rectangular travel bag'), combining スーツ ('suit') and ケース ('case').

ホテル.etymology: Borrowed in the Meiji era from English hotel (ultimately from French hôtel) to distinguish Western-style hotels from traditional Japanese inns (旅館).

タクシー.etymology: Borrowed in the Taishō era from English taxi, itself clipped from taximeter cab.

テーブル.etymology: Borrowed from English table to name a raised dining or café table used with chairs, in contrast with low floor tables.

バター.etymology: Borrowed in the Meiji period from English butter as Western dairy and baking spread across Japan.

ミルク.etymology: Borrowed from English milk; in everyday Japanese ミルク often refers to milk added to coffee or tea, alongside Sino-Japanese 牛乳 for fresh drinking milk.

ドア.etymology: Borrowed from English door, referring specifically to a hinged or automatic Western-style door rather than a sliding Japanese 戸 (to) or 襖 (fusuma).

カフェ.etymology: Borrowed from French café ('coffeehouse'), first popularized in late Meiji and Taishō cities and revived in contemporary Japanese for neighborhood coffeehouses.

ランプ.etymology: Borrowed from Dutch lamp and English lamp in the nineteenth century, initially for oil and kerosene lamps and later for electric desk and reading lamps.

ポケット.etymology: Borrowed from English pocket with Western tailored clothing in the Meiji era.

シャワー.etymology: Borrowed from English shower (short for shower bath).

パイプ.etymology: Borrowed from English pipe for both plumbing/heating tubes and smoking pipes.

ピアノ.etymology: Borrowed via English and Italian piano (short for Italian pianoforte, 'soft-loud').

旅館.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 旅 ('travel, journey') and 館 ('hall, mansion, lodging house'), naming a traditional Japanese inn.

電話.etymology: Meiji-era Sino-Japanese coinage (wasei-kango) combining 電 ('lightning, electricity') and 話 ('speech, conversation') to translate English telephone.

電車.etymology: Modern Sino-Japanese compound of 電 ('electricity') and 車 ('wheeled vehicle, carriage'), coined for electric streetcars and commuter trains.

時間.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 時 ('time, hour, season') and 間 ('interval, space between'), denoting either a span of hours or time in general.

時計.etymology: Compound of 時 ('time, hour') and 計 ('measure, gauge'). Historically read どけい from 土圭 ('sundial') and reanalyzed with 計 ('timepiece, meter') as tokei.

天気.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 天 ('sky, heavens') and 気 ('air, breath, atmospheric vapor'), meaning atmospheric weather.

元気.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 元 ('origin, foundation') and 気 ('vital energy, breath'), originally referring to the fundamental life force of nature and people, and in everyday speech meaning 'lively, healthy, in good spirits'.

history.meaning: primordial vitality; good health and spirits

安心.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 安 ('peaceful, settled, safe') and 心 ('heart, mind'), literally 'a settled heart'—feeling relieved and free from worry.

予約.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 予 ('beforehand, in advance') and 約 ('promise, agreement'), meaning an advance booking or reservation.

紅茶.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 紅 ('crimson, deep red') and 茶 ('tea'), named after the coppery-red color of oxidized black tea liquor (just as Chinese hóngchá literally means 'red tea').

牛乳.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 牛 ('cow, cattle') and 乳 ('milk'), literally 'cow's milk'.

玄関.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 玄 ('deep, profound') and 関 ('gate, barrier'). Originally a Zen Buddhist term for the gateway to profound teachings and the formal entry hall of a temple, it generalized to the entranceway of Japanese homes and inns where shoes are removed.

駅.etymology: From Sino-Japanese 駅 (traditional 驛, eki), which in the ancient Ritsuryō highway system named post-horse relay stations spaced along imperial roads; in the Meiji railway era it was adopted for train stations.

鍵.etymology: Native Japanese word *kagi*, related to 鉤 ('hook') from the hooked metal bar used to draw or lift wooden latches in early Japanese doors, later applied to keys and locks.

部屋.etymology: Native Japanese compound of 部 (*he*, 'partition, divided section') with rendaku voicing + 屋 (*ya*, 'roof, chamber, house'), literally 'a partitioned-off chamber'.

名前.etymology: Native Japanese compound of 名 (*na*, 'name') and 前 (*mae*, 'front, presence, assigned portion'), originally polite or formal and now the standard everyday noun for 'name'.

手紙.etymology: Native Japanese compound of 手 (*te*, 'hand, handwriting') and 紙 (*kami* -> *-gami* via rendaku, 'paper'), shifting from a handy slip of note paper to any written letter.

新しい.etymology: Inherited from Old Japanese *aratasi* ('fresh, new'), which underwent consonant metathesis (*r...t* > *t...r*) in the Heian period to become *atarasi* > modern 新しい (*atarashii*).

静か.etymology: Native Japanese na-adjective built from the ancient root *sidu-* ('calm, settled, sunken', also seen in 沈む *shizumu*, 'sink, settle') plus the descriptive suffix *-ka*.

おはようございます.etymology: Polite morning greeting formed from honorific prefix お + the western/polite *-u* adverbial sound change (ウ音便) of 早い (*hayaku* > *hayō*, 'early') + polite verb ございます: literally 'It is early!'

sources.title: Wiktionary — おはようございます (Japanese)

ありがとうございます.etymology: Formed from the adjective 有り難い (*arigatai*, from 有り 'exist' + 難い 'hard, difficult': 'rare, precious, hard to come by') via the *-ku > -u* adverbial sound change (*arigataku* > *arigatō*) plus polite ございます.

history.form: ありがとうございます

sources.title: Wiktionary — ありがとうございます (Japanese)

写真.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 写 ('copy, depict') and 真 ('truth, the real thing'): 'copying the true likeness'. It first named painted portraits of deities and nobles; in the late Edo period it also meant drawing from life, and when photographs arrived from the West at the end of the Edo period it was adopted as the translation of English 'photograph', gradually replacing rivals such as 写真絵 and 照画.

history.meaning: portrait of a deity or noble person

sources.title: Shogakukan: Selected Nihon Kokugo Daijiten — 写真 (語誌)

音楽.etymology: Sino-Japanese word borrowed from Middle Chinese 音樂 ('music'), built from 音 ('sound') and 楽 (old form 樂, 'music; enjoyment').

メートル.etymology: Borrowed from French mètre, the metric unit of length. Japanese also has the doublet メーター, from English 'meter', which now usually means a measuring instrument; the old kanji spellings were 米 and 米突.

スイッチ.etymology: Borrowed from English 'switch', a device that turns an electric current on and off; Japanese also uses it for railway points and, as スイッチする, for changing one's approach.

市場.etymology: Compound of 市 ('market, town trade gathering') and 場 ('place, ground'). Read いちば for a physical food or street market where goods change hands directly, and しじょう in broader economic or municipal market contexts.

中庭.etymology: Native Japanese compound (jukujikun/kun-reading) of 中 ('inside, inner') and 庭 ('garden, courtyard'), naming an enclosed courtyard surrounded by wings or walls of a house or inn.

蜂蜜.etymology: Sino-Japanese / hybrid compound written with 蜂 ('bee') and 蜜 ('nectar, honey'), combining native kun reading はち ('bee') with Sino-Japanese みつ ('honey').

鉛筆.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 鉛 ('lead') and 筆 ('writing brush'), originally referring to leaden styluses in classical Chinese and adopted in Edo-Meiji Japan for Western graphite pencils.

現金.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 現 ('present, on the spot, actual') and 金 ('money, gold'), literally 'money right in front of you' as opposed to credit or ledger accounts.

土曜日.etymology: Compound of 土曜 ('Saturn day', associated with the Five Phases element 土 'earth') and 日 ('day'), part of the seven-day week standardized officially in Meiji-era Japan in 1876.

morphemes.meaning: celestial luminary; day of the week

木曜日.etymology: Compound of 木曜 ('Jupiter day', linked to the Five Phases element 木 'wood/tree') and 日 ('day') in the traditional East Asian planetary week.

水曜日.etymology: Compound of 水曜 ('Mercury day', linked to the Five Phases element 水 'water') and 日 ('day') in the seven-day week.

金曜日.etymology: Compound of 金曜 ('Venus day', linked to the Five Phases element 金 'metal/gold') and 日 ('day') in the seven-day planetary week.

陶器.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 陶 ('kiln-fired pottery, mould clay') and 器 ('vessel, implement'), designating glazed earthenware and stoneware vessels.

受け皿.etymology: Native compound of 受ける ('receive, catch, support') in stem form 受け and 皿 ('plate, dish', voiced to ざら by rendaku), literally 'a dish that catches a cup above it'.

割引.etymology: Compound of 割り ('tenth-part proportion, rate', from 割る 'divide') and 引き ('pulling back, subtracting', from 引く), literally 'subtracting a proportion off the price'.

看板.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 看 ('look at, watch') and 板 ('wooden board'), originally a painted wooden shop board hung outside to catch passers-by's eyes.

新聞紙.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 新聞 ('newspaper', literally 'newly heard things') and 紙 ('paper'), referring specifically to sheets of newsprint.

半額.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 半 ('half') and 額 ('monetary amount, stated sum'), literally 'half the stated sum'.

注文.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 注 ('pour, fix attention, annotate') and 文 ('writing, document'), which shifted in medieval/early-modern Japanese commerce from 'an itemized written list' to 'placing an order for goods'.

値段.etymology: Compound of native 値 (ね, 'value, worth') and Sino-Japanese 段 (だん, 'step, grade, level'), literally 'the level of worth' of an item.

配達.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 配 ('distribute, allot') and 達 ('reach, deliver to a destination'), coined for modern postal and goods delivery.

眼鏡.etymology: Jukujikun spelling pairing 眼 ('eye') + 鏡 ('mirror, lens') with native reading めがね (from 目 'eye' + 金 'metal frame').

椅子.etymology: Borrowed from Middle/Early Mandarin Chinese 椅子 ('chair'), combining 椅 ('chair, catalpa wood') and noun suffix 子, retaining the Tang-Song reading いす.

真鍮.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 真 ('true, pure') and 鍮 ('brass, copper-zinc alloy'), attested from the Muromachi and Edo periods for golden-yellow brass hardware.

電線.etymology: Sino-Japanese Meiji compound of 電 ('electricity, lightning') and 線 ('thread, wire, line'), created for telegraph and electrical power wiring.

脚立.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 脚 ('leg, support') and 立 ('stand'), originally a standing wooden trestle or footstool and now the standard word for a folding A-frame stepladder.

楽譜.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 楽 ('music') and 譜 ('chronicle, systematic chart, notation'), denoting written musical notation or a score.

音符.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 音 ('sound, tone') and 符 ('tally mark, written symbol'), literally 'a symbol marking a musical pitch and duration'.

白紙.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound of 白 ('white, unmarked') and 紙 ('paper'), denoting an unwritten sheet of paper and figuratively a clean slate.

宿帳.etymology: Hybrid Japanese compound of native 宿 (やど, 'inn, lodging') and Sino-Japanese 帳 (ちょう, 'bound register book'), the traditional guest ledger kept at travellers' inns since the Edo period.

屋根裏.etymology: Native Japanese compound of 屋根 ('roof', itself 屋 'house' + 根 'covering/base') and 裏 ('underside, back'), literally 'the space underneath the roof'.

市役所.etymology: Sino-Japanese administrative compound of 市 ('incorporated city') and 役所 ('public office', from 役 'official duty' + 所 'place'), designating municipal City Hall.

買い物.etymology: Native Japanese compound of 買い (stem of 買う 'to buy') and 物 (もの, 'things, goods'), attested from early-modern townspeople speech for everyday shopping.

雨戸.etymology: Transparent native Japanese (和語) compound joining あま- (the bound combining form of 雨 あめ, 'rain') and 戸 (と, 'door, sliding shutter').
雨戸.notes: Traditional exterior wooden storm shutters that slide or swing closed to protect glass or paper windows from wind and rain.

雨粒.etymology: Native Japanese compound of あま- (bound form of 雨 あめ, 'rain') and 粒 (つぶ, 'round drop, grain, bead').
雨粒.notes: Shares the older combining vowel あま- seen in 雨戸 ('storm shutter') and 雨傘 ('umbrella').

稲妻.etymology: Poetic native compound 稲妻 (いなずま), combining 稲 (いな-, bound form of いね 'rice plant') and 妻 (つま, 'spouse, partner', voiced to -ずま by rendaku).
稲妻.notes: Coined in ancient Japan because late-summer lightning storms coincided with the ripening of rice ears, inspiring the belief that lightning wedded and fertilized the rice crop.

蝶番.etymology: Compound 蝶番 (ちょうつがい), combining Sino-Japanese 蝶 (ちょう, 'butterfly') with native 番 (つがい, 'interlocking pair, joint').
蝶番.notes: Named from the two flat metal leaves of an open hinge resembling the spread wings of a butterfly.

鍵盤.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 鍵盤 (けんばん), uniting 鍵 ('key, lock bolt') and 盤 ('flat board, tray').
鍵盤.notes: Used both for the full keyboard of a piano or organ and for individual keys along the row.

土砂降り.etymology: Hybrid compound joining Sino-Japanese 土砂 (どしゃ, 'earth and gravel') with native 降り (ふり -> -ぶり via rendaku, from 降る 'fall, pour down').
土砂降り.notes: Likens a blinding cloudburst to earth and stones pouring straight out of the sky.

鼻歌.etymology: Transparent native Japanese compound of 鼻 (はな, 'nose') and 歌 (うた, 'song').
鼻歌.notes: Describes humming a melody softly through closed lips while working or walking.

紙やすり.etymology: Native compound of 紙 (かみ, 'paper') and やすり (鑢, 'metal file or rasp').
紙やすり.notes: Literally a 'paper file'—heavy paper coated with abrasive grit for smoothing wood before painting.

台所.etymology: Compound 台所 (だいどころ), joining 台 (だい, 'raised stand or tray table for preparing food') and 所 (ところ -> -どころ by rendaku, 'place').
台所.notes: Originated in aristocratic households for the room where meal stands (台盤) were arranged; became the universal warm home word for 'kitchen'.

切符.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 切符 (きっぷ, with gemination from きりふ), combining 切 ('cut, notch') and 符 ('tally slip, voucher').
切符.notes: Originally denoted a wooden or paper tally cut in two as proof of payment; adopted in the Meiji railway era for train and theatre tickets.

はがき.etymology: Native Japanese compound 葉書 (はがき), from 葉 (は, 'leaf, small slip') and 書き (かき -> -がき by rendaku, 'writing').
はがき.notes: Originally referred to brief notes jotted on single slips of paper (端書き / 葉書き), standardized for postal cards in modern Japan.

調律.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 調律 (ちょうりつ), uniting 調 ('harmonize, adjust') and 律 ('standard pitch pipe, musical law').
調律.notes: Refers specifically to bringing musical strings or pipes into exact pitch harmony.

作曲家.etymology: Three-character Sino-Japanese compound 作曲家 (さっきょくか): 作 ('make, create') + 曲 ('melody, piece of music') + specialist suffix -家 ('master, professional').
作曲家.notes: Shares 曲 with 楽曲 and specialist suffix -家 with 建築家 ('architect').

天気予報.etymology: Four-character Sino-Japanese compound 天気予報 (てんきよほう), pairing 天気 ('weather', literally 'sky energy') with 予報 ('advance report, forecast').
天気予報.notes: Coined in the Meiji meteorological service and used daily in broadcasts and conversation.

未完成.etymology: Sino-Japanese prefix 未- (み-, 'not yet') attached to 完成 (かんせい, 'completion': 完 'whole' + 成 'accomplish').
未完成.notes: Unlike 不- ('non-'), 未- implies work begun that has not yet reached its intended finish.

再開.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 再開 (さいかい), from 再 ('again, a second time') and 開 ('open, begin').
再開.notes: Used when an inn, shop, or concert series opens its doors again after an interruption.

移動.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 移動 (いどう), combining 移 ('shift, transfer') and 動 ('move').
移動.notes: Covers shifting furniture across a room as well as travelling between places.

湿気.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 湿気 (colloquially read しっけ with gemination, alongside しっき), from 湿 ('damp, moist') and 気 ('air, vapour').
湿気.notes: Central everyday word during Japan's rainy season when wooden doors and piano actions absorb moisture.

羊毛.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 羊毛 (ようもう), combining 羊 ('sheep') and 毛 ('hair, fleece, wool').
羊毛.notes: Dense compressed sheep's wool (羊毛フェルト) gives piano hammers their warm, rounded strike.

真夜中.etymology: Native Japanese prefix 真- (ま-, 'true, exact, dead centre') + 夜中 (よなか, 'middle of the night': 夜 よ + 中 なか).
真夜中.notes: Parallel to 真ん中 ('right in the middle') and 真夏 ('midsummer').

鋼.etymology: Native Japanese contraction はがね from 刃金 (は 'blade edge' + かね 'metal'), written with the single character 鋼 ('tempered steel').
鋼.notes: Originally denoted the hard carbon-steel edge forged into tools and swords; now used for high-tensile piano wire as well.

ピンセット.etymology: Borrowed in the late Edo / early Meiji period from Dutch pincet ('tweezers'), itself from French pincette (diminutive of pince, 'pincers').
ピンセット.notes: Entered Japanese through Dutch medical and scientific studies (蘭学) and remains the everyday word for precision tweezers.

バケツ.etymology: Borrowed from English bucket (reflecting English plural buckets or palatalized final -t -> -tsu).
バケツ.notes: Replaced wooden pails (桶 おけ) for everyday metal and plastic household buckets.

スポンジ.etymology: Borrowed from English sponge, ultimately from Ancient Greek σπογγιά (spongiá).
スポンジ.notes: Used both for kitchen/window sponges and sponge cake (スポンジケーキ).

フェルト.etymology: Borrowed from English felt, denoting non-woven cloth matted together from wool fibres by heat and moisture.
フェルト.notes: Essential inside upright and grand pianos for hammers, dampers, and action bushings.

オクターブ.etymology: Borrowed from French/English octave, from Latin octāva ('eighth'), naming the eight-note span of a diatonic scale.
オクターブ.notes: Standard term across Japanese piano instruction and acoustics.

ビスケット.etymology: Borrowed from English biscuit (compare 16th-century Portuguese loan ビスカウト), ultimately from Latin bis coctus ('twice baked').
ビスケット.notes: Refers to crisp tea biscuits baked to hold well beside hot tea or coffee.

アーモンド.etymology: Borrowed from English almond, tracing back through Old French almande to Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amygdálē).
アーモンド.notes: Ground almond meal (アーモンドプードル / アーモンド生地) is prized in Japanese pastry shops for tart crusts.

オリーブオイル.etymology: Compound loanword from English olive oil (オリーブ + オイル).
オリーブオイル.notes: Coexists with older Sino-hybrid オリーブ油 (オリーブゆ) in home cooking and cafés.

レンズ豆.etymology: Partial calque combining English/German loan レンズ ('lens', ultimately from Latin lēns, 'lentil') with native 豆 (まめ, 'bean, pulse').
レンズ豆.notes: Optics borrowed Latin lēns ('lentil') for glass lenses because of their curved lentil shape, and Japanese named the legume 'lens-bean' in turn!

扇風機.etymology: Meiji/Taishō Sino-Japanese coinage 扇風機 (せんぷうき), combining 扇 ('fan, stir breeze'), 風 ('wind'), and 機 ('machine').
扇風機.notes: Coined in Japan for early electric fans and adopted across East Asia (compare Korean 선풍기).

刷毛.etymology: Native Japanese noun はけ (related to 掃く はく, 'to sweep, brush across'), spelled with semantic ateji 刷毛 ('brushing-hair').
刷毛.notes: Refers to wide flat brushes used in carpentry, painting, dyeing, and pastry glazing.

老眼鏡.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 老眼鏡 (ろうがんきょう), joining 老眼 ('farsightedness of age') with 鏡 ('mirror, optical lens').
老眼鏡.notes: Shares 眼鏡 ('glasses, spectacles') with everyday めがね.

菩提樹.etymology: Compound of 菩提 (ぼだい, phonetic transcription of Sanskrit bodhi, 'awakening') and 樹 (じゅ, 'tree').
菩提樹.notes: Applied in Japanese botany and German lied translations (Schubert's Der Lindenbaum -> 菩提樹) to the heart-leaved linden tree.

木目.etymology: Hybrid reading もくめ combining Sino-Japanese 木 (もく, 'wood, timber') with native 目 (め, 'eye, pattern, grain').
木目.notes: Native 目 productively denotes fine surface patterns in 網目 ('mesh'), 織り目 ('weave'), and 木目 ('wood grain').

時計職人.etymology: Compound joining 時計 (とけい, 'clock, watch') and 職人 (しょくにん, 'skilled artisan, master craftsperson').
時計職人.notes: Evokes precision handiwork with tiny pins, springs, and tweezers.

和音.etymology: Sino-Japanese musical compound 和音 (わおん), from 和 ('harmony, blending together') and 音 ('musical tone').
和音.notes: Standard term for a musical chord sounded simultaneously on piano or strings.

鋼鉄.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 鋼鉄 (こうてつ), uniting 鋼 ('hardened steel') and 鉄 ('iron').
鋼鉄.notes: Pairs with single-character native/Sino 鋼 (はがね, 'tempered steel').

提灯.etymology: Muromachi-period tōon (唐音, Song/Ming Chinese) borrowing 提灯 (ちょうちん, originally ていちん), literally 'hand-carried lamp' (提 'carry in hand' + 灯 'lantern').
提灯.notes: Its tōon reading ちょうちん (rather than kan'on ていとう) marks its arrival with medieval Zen and merchant trade.

間取り図.etymology: Hybrid architectural compound joining native 間取り (まどり, from 間 'room/bay' + 取り 'arranging') with Sino-Japanese 図 (ず, 'diagram, plan').
間取り図.notes: Traditional Japanese rooms were laid out by tatami-module bays (間 ま), giving 間取り for any floor layout.

小雨.etymology: Native Japanese compound 小雨 (こさめ), from prefix 小- (こ-, 'light, small') + 雨 (あめ, 'rain') with historical medial consonant insertion (-s-).
小雨.notes: The same archaic euphonic -s- before 雨 (あめ -> さめ) appears in 春雨 (はるさめ, 'gentle spring rain') and 秋雨 (あきさめ).

生演奏.etymology: Hybrid compound combining native prefix 生- (なま-, 'unprocessed, live, in person') with Sino-Japanese 演奏 (えんそう, 'musical performance').
生演奏.notes: Contrasts live acoustic music with recorded playback.

一言一句.etymology: Four-character Sino-Japanese idiom (四字熟語) 一言一句 (いちごんいっく), pairing 一言 ('a single word') and 一句 ('a single phrase').
一言一句.notes: Uses traditional go'on reading ごん for 言 in set classical expressions.

踏み台.etymology: Hybrid compound of native 踏み (ふみ, masu-stem of 踏む 'to step on') and Sino-Japanese 台 (だい, 'platform, stand').
踏み台.notes: Denotes a low wooden stepstool kept in kitchens and shops for reaching high shelves.

足首.etymology: Transparent native Japanese anatomical compound of 足 (あし, 'foot, leg') and 首 (くび, 'neck, narrowed joint').
足首.notes: Parallel to 手首 (てくび, 'wrist', literally 'hand-neck').

夜明け.etymology: Native Japanese compound 夜明け (よあけ), from 夜 (よ, 'night') and 明け (あけ, nominalized stem of 明ける 'to grow light, dawn').
夜明け.notes: Evokes the transition from night darkness to first morning light.

海塩.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 海塩 (かいえん), from 海 ('sea, ocean') and 塩 ('salt').
海塩.notes: Distinguishes evaporated sea salt from rock salt (岩塩 がんえん).

定規.etymology: Sino-Japanese compound 定規 (じょうぎ), from 定 ('fix, establish') and 規 ('compass, standard rule').
定規.notes: Originally denoted carpenter's measuring standards before becoming the everyday word for a straightedge ruler.

表門.etymology: Hybrid compound joining native 表 (おもて, 'front, facing the street') with Sino-Japanese 門 (もん, 'gate').
表門.notes: Contrasts with 裏門 (うらもん, 'back gate') in traditional Japanese inns and houses.

小窓.etymology: Native Japanese compound of prefix 小- (こ-, 'small') and 窓 (まど, 'window').
小窓.notes: Used for high transom windows and small ventilation casements.

羽根板.etymology: Native Japanese compound of 羽根 (はね, 'feather, wing-like blade') and 板 (いた, 'wooden board').
羽根板.notes: Describes angled overlapping wooden slats on louvred shutters.

石壁.etymology: Native Japanese compound of 石 (いし, 'stone') and 壁 (かべ, 'wall').
石壁.notes: Refers to dressed stone courtyard or garden walls.

コンロ.etymology: Edo-period Sino-Japanese kitchen word 焜炉 (こんろ, combining 焜 'bright flame' + 炉 'hearth/brazier'), influenced in use by Dutch komfoor ('portable brazier').
コンロ.notes: Today written in katakana コンロ for gas and induction kitchen stoves.

グラニュー糖.etymology: Hybrid Meiji culinary compound clipping English granulated (sugar) to グラニュー and attaching Sino-Japanese 糖 (とう, 'sugar').
グラニュー糖.notes: Refers to fine, dry, free-flowing white crystals prized in pastry baking.

ペダル.etymology: Borrowed from English pedal, ultimately from Latin pedālis ('of the foot', from pēs, pedis 'foot').
ペダル.notes: Used for upright and grand piano foot pedals as well as bicycle pedals.

ラベル.etymology: Borrowed via Dutch label / early English spelling pronunciation, rather than later English /ˈleɪbəl/ (which separately gave レーベル for record labels).
ラベル.notes: Everyday Japanese distinguishes ラベル (paper jar or bottle label) from レーベル (music/publishing imprint).

トレイ.etymology: Borrowed from English tray, tracing back to Old English trīg ('wooden board or shallow dish').
トレイ.notes: Also spelled トレー; standard word in cafés and bakeries for baking and serving trays.

フロント.etymology: Japanese hospitality clipping (和製英語 shortening) from English front desk / front office.
フロント.notes: Standard word at both Western hotels and modernised ryokan for the reception counter.

クッション.etymology: Borrowed from English cushion, from Old French coissin.
クッション.notes: Refers to soft seat cushions on wooden café chairs as well as mechanical shock-absorbing pads.

シェフ.etymology: Borrowed from French chef (short for chef de cuisine, 'head of the kitchen').
シェフ.notes: Used both as a standalone noun and as a warm respectful title after a baker's or cook's name.
